newsitem.title: USA: Congress must help nation's capital, Gingrich says.
newsitem.headline: Congress must help nation's capital, Gingrich says.

text.p: Newly reelected House Speaker Newt Gingrich on Tuesday joined President Clinton in a pledge to restore pride in the nation's rundown, crime-ridden capital.
"We should not be ashamed to go back home and say you're darned right, we are helping our national capital," the Georgia Republican told House members after accepting the speakership.

Clinton last month promised help to the financially struggling District of Columbia, noting that its unusual status as a city without fiscal aid from a state had left it floundering in "a series of purgatories." He is expected to announce federal assistance in his State of the Union address Feb. 5.

First Lady Hillary Rodham Clinton also adopted the capital's cause, donating proceeds from the sale of her book to a children's hospital and participating in private efforts to help the city. Mrs. Clinton's aides said recently she planned to remain engaged in District of Columbia issues.
Gingrich said Congress needed to live up to its responsibility of assisting the District of Columbia so that voters would feel proud when they visited.
"We want you to know that you can say to anyone, anywhere in the world, come to America and visit Washington," Gingrich said. "It is a great city."
Gingrich said Congress was beginning to make real progress in helping the District, despite difficulties.

"It has to be done carefully. It cannot violate the citizens of this city," he said. "But let's be candid, this is our national capital and we have a unique obligation on both sides of the aisle to care about Washington."
Gingrich said some people thought he had lost his mind when he told Washington Mayor Marion Barry 18 months ago that he wanted Washington to be the "finest capital city in the world."
The speaker said he continued to believe that.

"We owe it to every child of this District to have a decent chance to go to a school that succeeds in a neighborhood that is drug free and safe, with the expectation of getting a job in a community that actually cares about them and provides a better future," Gingrich said.
The district, which had a $90 million budget shortfall in fiscal year 1996, was subjected to the oversight of a five-member financial board created by Congress in 1995.
The board released a plan last month asking the federal government to pitch in up to $1 billion in Medicaid and other aid to help the city.
Behind its tourist attractions -- the White House, the monuments and the museums -- Washington is a deeply troubled city of 543,000 people, many poor and black.
The city is short of firetrucks and emergency vehicles; police cars go unrepaired, potholes unfilled; crime flourishes; and a former army general has been appointed to run its schools.
